title.en: Quiet paws over city and harbour

text.en: Six short unrhymed lines can hold an entire movie scene: pale mist glides silently over water and rooftops, pauses politely, and vanishes without making a sound.

Carl Sandburg's Fog is one of the shortest, most memorable poems in the textbook—just six crisp lines written in free verse without any fixed rhyme scheme or regular beat.
From start to finish, Sandburg builds a single extended metaphor (plus subtle personification): 'The fog comes on little cat feet.'
Think why a cat fits fog so well: cats enter rooms completely noiselessly without announcing themselves, just as cool mist drifts across land and water.
Then the fog 'sits looking over harbour and city on silent haunches'—the exact crouching posture of a watchful cat surveying its surroundings calmly without disturbing anything.
Just as suddenly and mysteriously, 'and then moves on'. Nature's changes do not ask permission or create drama; they arrive softly, pause briefly, and vanish cleanly.

caption.en: Trace imagery, tone and central idea

text.en: Carl Sandburg's poem Fog is only six lines long, yet it paints an unforgettable picture of how winter mist moves.
He opens directly with the image: the fog arrives 'on little cat feet'.
Instead of using 'like' or 'as', he merges fog and cat completely, forming an extended metaphor across all six lines.
Why compare fog to a cat rather than an elephant or storm? Because cats move softly without footsteps or warning.
Next, the fog 'sits looking over harbour and city', watching ships, cranes, rooftops, and streets underneath.
Notice how the word 'looking' also hints at personification, giving thick mist quiet observant eyes.
The phrase 'on silent haunches' captures how a cat folds its hind legs and rests watchfully before leaving.
Mist behaves identically: it hangs thickly over city buildings for an hour without rushing or roaring.
Then comes the brief third movement: 'and then moves on'—three simple words ending the poem.
Nothing dramatic stops the fog, and nothing chases it away; when sunlight or wind shifts, it glides softly out.
Examine the form: Fog is written in free verse, meaning there is no end rhyme and no strict syllable count.
Line breaks happen naturally after small pauses, matching the slow drifting pace of mist across water.
Imagery appeals chiefly to sight and stillness: harbour water, city skyline, soft footsteps, crouched posture.
In just twenty-one words, Sandburg shows how ordinary weather feels alive when observed closely.

problem.en: Explain why Fog uses an extended metaphor instead of a simile, and trace its three actions.

text.en: Step 1 (Arrival): 'comes on little cat feet' stresses noiseless, subtle entry.

why.en: Direct metaphor blends cat and mist seamlessly without 'like'.

text.en: Step 2 (Pause): 'sits looking over harbour and city on silent haunches'.

why.en: Personification makes mist feel watchful yet calm.

text.en: Step 3 (Exit): 'and then moves on' shows impermanence.

why.en: Free verse without rhyme matches spontaneous natural rhythm.

prompt.en: Give three reasons why comparing fog to a cat works well, and explain what free verse means here.

requiredIdeas.en: Cats arrive silently on soft paws just like noiseless mist
A cat sitting on haunches watches quietly like lingering fog over city and harbour
Free verse uses no fixed rhyme or metre, matching natural unhurried movement

commonMisconceptions.en: Saying the poem has an abab rhyme scheme

points.en: Carl Sandburg compares fog directly to a cat across six unrhymed lines.
The three-step motion—silent arrival, watchful pause on haunches, smooth departure—captures mist perfectly.
Key devices: extended metaphor, personification ('sits looking'), and visual imagery.
Written in free verse, the poem creates calm wonder using just twenty-one simple words.
